I
Let us first examine the individual beatitudes and con-
sider whether we are among those addressed.
"Blessed are the poor in spirit." What does it mean to be
poor in spirit? It means to realize one's poverty in the
presence of God. No doubt in virtue of our essential nature
as men we are all poor in the sight of God, helpless and frail,
weak and perishable mortals. The point is, however—do we
realize this fact? Do we realize it, not in the sense of theor-
etical knowledge, but in such a way that this awareness
penetrates our whole being and informs our whole way of life?
To be poor in spirit means not to conceal the essential
poverty of our human nature by the apparent wealth which
a man may acquire. It may be a question of outward
prosperity; as Luther says, to be poor in spirit means "a
heart which does not cleave to property and wealth, but,
even when a man has it, it is for him as though he had it
not". Whether we are spiritually poor in this sense may be
tested by consideration of another comment of Luther: "It is
not that a man is asked to leave house and home, wife and
child, and wander through the land to be a burden to
others ... but the meaning rather refers to the Christian who
can in heart leave house and home, wife and child, even
though he actually remains with them, sups with them, and
serves them out of love, as God has commanded; and yet
his disposition is such that, when need arises, he can for the
fulfilment of God's will abandon it all at any time. If you
are so minded, then you have left all, so let not your heart
cleave to earthly things, but remain pure from greed, and
free from too much attachment to this world... and in fact
a rich man may wish to be spiritually poor yet he is not for
